Past Continuous in Affirmative
We use the past continuous tense to describe events that took place for a period of time in the past.

Past continuous helps to describe the setting or environment in a story: “She knocked on the door and the dog was barking.”

 This tense is also used to talk about an action interrupted by another action. Example:

I was reading and my aunt asked me for help.

 

Use the past continuous to talk about simultaneous actions in the past. Example:

I was watching TV while she was preparing breakfast.

 

In order to make an affirmative sentence using the past continuous, follow this structure:

 Subject + verb to be in past + verb ending in –ing + complement.

 I was reading about the history of programming languages.

Understanding What Coordination is
Have you ever had problems when writing a text because you don't know how to connect ideas? Well, there is a process in writing called coordination. Let's see how it can help you.

Let’s consider the next two sentences:

  1. Programming languages are necessary for software development.
  1. They translate instructions to a machine.

How can we connect these two ideas? Let’s see:

Programming languages are necessary for software development, for they translate instructions to a machine.

We use conjunctions, like for to join two complete sentences in order to make writing more fluent. In the chart below, you’re going to find a group of coordinating conjunctions that can be very useful:

images.text: I'm going to talk about a presentation I attended in the Computer Science Fair. I was wandering around the school campus when I saw this poster saying “Programming Languages Hall of Fame”, so I immediately wanted to see what it was about. As if they were rock stars, all the profiles of the people involved in the development of programming languages were exposed.

Here, you'll find a glimpse of some of those important people in computer science, but first, let's remark upon some basic concepts. Programming languages are used to communicate instructions to a machine; they also make algorithms visible. A long time ago, computers didn't need these languages, for decimal or binary forms were the paths for communicating orders.
The first profile that I read was from Charles Babbage (1791-1811), an English mathematician who created the concept of a computer that can be programmed. His invention is the benchmark of programming languages. When I was reading about him, I couldn't believe my eyes because I thought all the inventions related to computers were made in the 20th century.

German engineer Konrad Zuse (1910-1995) was another important figure, he invented the first programmable computer, the Z3. What I like about this machine is that it had two predecessors, which means that it didn't appear out of the blue. Talking about more recent contributions, in 1949 John Mauchly (1907-1980) developed the Short Code, which was the first higher-level language made for an electronic computer.
From Alan Cooper (1952), the creator of Visual Basic, to Guido van Rossum (1956), the inventor of Python, all these people have been essential for the development and evolution of programming languages. I'm writing this blog entry thanks to them since programming languages make every move in a computer possible. What do you think about this post? Leave your comments!
